content.text:
You're right on both counts. CodeRabbit's `-DisableCache` suggestion goes against how Maester is meant to work. And `Get-MtDirectoryRoleMember` is almost entirely a copy of `Get-MtRoleMember`.

## Places that skip the cache during a run (on main)

**Checks that pass `-DisableCache` themselves (13):**

| Check | Request |
|---|---|
| CIS.M365.5.1.2.2, 5.1.2.3, 5.1.4.6, 5.1.5.1, 5.1.6.2 | `policies/authorizationPolicy`. The same request five times, and every one goes to Graph again. |
| CIS.M365.1.3.4 | `admin/appsAndServices/settings` |
| CIS.M365.1.3.5 | `admin/forms/settings` |
| CIS.M365.1.3.7 | `servicePrincipals` filtered to one appId |
| CIS.M365.4.1 | `deviceManagement/settings` |
| CIS.M365.5.1.5.2 | `policies/adminConsentRequestPolicy` |
| CIS.M365.5.2.3.5 | `policies/authenticationMethodsPolicy` |
| MT.1024 | `directory/recommendations?$expand=impactedResources` |
| MT.1059 | `security/identities/healthIssues` |

**Shared helpers:**
- **`Get-MtRoleMember.ps1:86`** calls `Get-MtDirectoryRoleAssignment … -DisableCache`. That affects eight checks: CIS 1.1.1 and 1.1.3, CISA AAD 7.1 to 7.3, MT.1020, MT.1189 and MT.1192. My commit `bd7eaf70d` on 17 October kept that switch only because it was already there; it had no reason of its own.
- **The new `Get-MtDirectoryRoleMember`** in #2601 copies the same `-DisableCache`.

**These can stay:**
- `Invoke-MtGraphRequest.ps1:175` skips the cache only for `nextLink` pages, because skip tokens repeat. The whole result is still cached afterwards.
- The `-DisableCache` and `-ClearCache` switches on `Invoke-MtGraphRequest`, `Get-MtConditionalAccessPolicy`, `Get-MtPrivateAccessApplication`, `Get-MdeConfiguration`, `Invoke-MtGitHubRequest` and `Get-MtSpo` are options a caller can choose. No check passes them.

**One thing to watch when removing the switch from `Get-MtRoleMember`.** It adds an `AssignmentType` property with `Add-Member -Force` to each principal object. Once those objects come from the cache, every caller would be changing the same shared objects. That's mostly harmless, because each call sets the value again, but it's worth a unit test.

## Get-MtRoleMember and Get-MtDirectoryRoleMember compared

Most of the new function's 53 lines are the same as the existing function:
- the same `Get-MtDirectoryRoleAssignment -ExpandPrincipal -DisableCache` call;
- the same loop;
- the same skip for an assignment with no principal;
- the same one-level group expansion.

What's different:
1. **Reading a group.** The new function calls `groups/{id}/members` directly. The existing one goes through `Get-MtGroupMember`, which first reads `groups/{id}`, then its members.
2. **The only real change: it throws on errors other than 404.** `Get-MtGroupMember` shows a warning and returns `$null` on any error, so the group's admins are silently left out.
3. **Things it drops:** there's no `-Role` by name and no `AssignmentType`, results aren't grouped or de-duplicated per role, and the group object itself isn't returned.

**Why the author did it this way.** CodeRabbit said a 403 on a group lets 1.1.4 pass without checking the admins in that group. The author didn't want to change `Get-MtGroupMember` or `Get-MtRoleMember` because they're public commands. They also took our earlier "keep shared behaviour unchanged" comment as applying here, though it was only about `Invoke-MtGraphRequest`. So they copied the function and changed one line's worth of behaviour.

**The real bug is in `Get-MtGroupMember`.** Turning a 403 into "no members" is a false pass for all eight checks above, not just the three CIS ones in #2601. The clean fix is to make `Get-MtGroupMember` throw on errors other than 404, keeping its fuller 404 and GDAP handling. function Test-MtGraphNotFoundError {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Internal: Returns whether a Microsoft Graph ErrorRecord is a 404 Not Found.

    .DESCRIPTION
    Checks the response status code in its enum, string and integer forms, then the exception's own StatusCode
    property, then the message, because the form depends on the Graph SDK and PowerShell version.
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([bool])]
    param(
        # The ErrorRecord caught from a Graph request.
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
        [System.Management.Automation.ErrorRecord]$ErrorRecord
    )

    $responseStatusCode = $ErrorRecord.Exception.Response.StatusCode
    $exceptionStatusCode = $ErrorRecord.Exception.StatusCode
    return ($responseStatusCode -eq [System.Net.HttpStatusCode]::NotFound) -or
        ($responseStatusCode -eq 'NotFound') -or
        ($responseStatusCode -eq 404) -or
        ($exceptionStatusCode -eq [System.Net.HttpStatusCode]::NotFound) -or
        ($ErrorRecord.Exception.Message -match 'NotFound|404')
}

Maester reports on one snapshot of a tenant. Every check in a run should read Graph through the session cache, so checks that ask for the same data see the same answer and the run doesn't send the same request again. Several checks and one shared helper skip the cache anyway.

**Checks that pass `-DisableCache` (13)**

| Check | Request |
| --- | --- |
| CIS.M365.5.1.2.2, 5.1.2.3, 5.1.4.6, 5.1.5.1, 5.1.6.2 | `policies/authorizationPolicy`, fetched again by each of the five |
| CIS.M365.1.3.4 | `admin/appsAndServices/settings` |
| CIS.M365.1.3.5 | `admin/forms/settings` |
| CIS.M365.1.3.7 | `servicePrincipals` filtered by appId |
| CIS.M365.4.1 | `deviceManagement/settings` |
| CIS.M365.5.1.5.2 | `policies/adminConsentRequestPolicy` |
| CIS.M365.5.2.3.5 | `policies/authenticationMethodsPolicy` |
| MT.1024 | `directory/recommendations?$expand=impactedResources` |
| MT.1059 | `security/identities/healthIssues` |

**Shared helper**

`Get-MtRoleMember` reads role assignments with `-DisableCache`, which affects every check that uses it (CIS 1.1.1 and 1.1.3, CISA MS.AAD.7.1 to 7.3, MT.1020, MT.1189, MT.1192).

**Group lookups hide read errors**

`Get-MtGroupMember` returns `$null` with a warning on any error reading a group, not only on 404. A 403 (missing `GroupMember.Read.All` or `Directory.Read.All`, a restricted administrative unit) or a 429 makes a group look empty, so a check that counts role holders or admins can pass without reading them. `Get-MtRoleMember` inherits this. A 404 (deleted group, external GDAP group) should still be skipped; anything else should stop the check with an error.

**What stays**

- `Invoke-MtGraphRequest` reads `nextLink` pages without the cache because skip tokens are not always unique; the whole result is still cached.
- Transport helpers that only offer a `DisableCache` switch to callers (`Invoke-MtGraphRequest`, `Invoke-MtGraphRequestCache`, `Get-MtDirectoryRoleAssignment`, `Get-MtConditionalAccessPolicy`, `Get-MtPrivateAccessApplication`, `Get-MdeConfiguration`, `Invoke-MtGitHubRequest`).

**Fix**

- Remove `-DisableCache` from the 13 checks and from `Get-MtRoleMember`.
- Make `Get-MtGroupMember` throw on errors other than 404, for the group, its members and nested groups.
- Add a unit test that fails when any check, pack or helper outside the allow list uses `DisableCache`, so new code can't bring it back.

Related: maester365/maester#2601 added a copy of `Get-MtRoleMember` to get the error behaviour; with this change it can use the shared command.
EOF

input.recap: Issue #2624 and PR #2625 are open: checks now read through the Graph cache, a unit test blocks new DisableCache uses, and group lookups throw on non-404 errors. I pushed 898dc4c to #2601 to drop the duplicate helper. CI hasn't finished on either PR.

content.text:
I've opened the issue and the PR, and pushed the clean-up to #2601. CI is still running on both PRs.

**Issue [#2624](https://github.com/maester365/maester/issues/2624)** lists the 13 checks and `Get-MtRoleMember` that turn the cache off, and `Get-MtGroupMember` treating any error as an empty group.

**PR [#2625](https://github.com/maester365/maester/pull/2625)** fixes #2624:
- **Cache:** `-DisableCache` is gone from the 13 checks and from `Get-MtRoleMember`. The five CIS checks that read `policies/authorizationPolicy` now share one request.
- **New unit test, `GraphCacheUsage.Tests.ps1`.** It reads every `.ps1` under `tests/`, `packs/`, `powershell/public` and `powershell/internal`. It fails on two things:
  - Any mention of `DisableCache` outside the allow list, other than in comments.
  - A bare `-DisableCache` passed from a file on the allow list. Only `Invoke-MtGraphRequest` may do that, for its `nextLink` pages.

  The allow list is the seven transport helpers that only offer the switch to their callers. Run against main, the test fails on all 14 places this PR fixes.
- **Group lookups:**
  - `Get-MtGroupMember` still skips a group that isn't found (404). It now throws on any other error reading the group, its members or a nested group, and `Get-MtRoleMember` inherits that.
  - The 404 check moved into a shared internal `Test-MtGraphNotFoundError`, so both lookups use the same logic.
  - New unit tests cover 404, 403 and 429, nested groups, and the cache.
- **Behaviour change:** `Get-MtGroupMember` and `Get-MtRoleMember` are public commands. A custom test calling them now gets an error, not an empty result, when a group can't be read. The PR description says so.
- **Unit tests:** 5,658 run. The only failure is the ZeroTrustAssessment test, which fails on your Mac because the module is installed there.

**#2601: I pushed `898dc4c` to the author's branch.**
- **Removed:** `Get-MtDirectoryRoleMember` and its tests.
- **Changed:** CIS 1.1.1, 1.1.3 and 1.1.4 use `Get-MtRoleMember` again. Their unit tests now mock it, and each has a test that the check errors when the role members can't be read.
- **Kept:** the author's other changes, such as the unique-user count and the empty-role guard.
- **Unit tests:** the same single local failure.
- **Merge #2625 first.** Until #2625 lands, the new .md lines in #2601 that say the check "reports an error" when a group can't be read aren't true yet.

**#2601 on the desk:** the card is a draft with an updated comment. The comment explains the push and points to #2625. It also asks the author not to add CodeRabbit's `-DisableCache`, and approves on the condition that #2625 merges first. Queue it when you're happy with the wording.

6.2.1 Ensure all forms of mail forwarding are blocked and/or
disabled (Automated)
Profile Applicability:
• E3 Level 1
• E5 Level 1
Description:
Exchange Online offers several methods of managing the flow of email messages.
These are Remote domain, Transport Rules, and Anti-spam outbound policies. These
methods work together to provide comprehensive coverage for potential automatic
forwarding channels:
• Outlook forwarding using inbox rules.
• Outlook forwarding configured using OOF rule.
• OWA forwarding setting (ForwardingSmtpAddress).
• Forwarding set by the admin using EAC (ForwardingAddress).
• Forwarding using Power Automate / Flow.
Ensure a Transport rule and Anti-spam outbound policy are used to block mail
forwarding.
NOTE: Any exclusions should be implemented based on organizational policy.
Rationale:
Attackers often create these rules to exfiltrate data from your tenancy, this could be
accomplished via access to an end-user account or otherwise. An insider could also use
one of these methods as a secondary channel to exfiltrate sensitive data.
Impact:
Care should be taken before implementation to ensure there is no business need for
case-by-case auto-forwarding. Disabling auto-forwarding to remote domains will affect
all users in an organization. Any exclusions should be implemented based on
organizational policy.
=====PAGE 432=====
Audit:
Note: Audit is a two step procedure as follows:
STEP 1: Transport rules
To audit using the UI:
1. Select Exchange to open the Exchange admin center.
2. Select Mail Flow then Rules.
3. Review the rules and verify that none of them are forwards or redirects e-mail to
external domains.
To audit using PowerShell:
1. Connect to Exchange online using Connect-ExchangeOnline.
2. Run the following PowerShell command to review the Transport Rules that are
redirecting email:
Get-TransportRule | Where-Object {$_.RedirectMessageTo -ne $null} | ft
Name,RedirectMessageTo
3. Verify that none of the addresses listed belong to external domains outside of the
organization. If nothing returns then there are no transport rules set to redirect
messages.
STEP 2: Anti-spam outbound policy
To audit using the UI:
1. Navigate to Microsoft 365 Defender https://security.microsoft.com/
2. Expand E-mail & collaboration then select Policies & rules.
3. Select Threat policies > Anti-spam.
4. Inspect Anti-spam outbound policy (default) and ensure Automatic
forwarding is set to Off - Forwarding is disabled
5. Inspect any additional custom outbound policies and ensure Automatic
forwarding is set to Off - Forwarding is disabled, in accordance with the
organization's exclusion policies.
To audit using PowerShell:
1. Connect to Exchange online using Connect-ExchangeOnline.
2. Run the following PowerShell cmdlet:
Get-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy | ft Name, AutoForwardingMode
3. In each outbound policy verify AutoForwardingMode is Off.
=====PAGE 433=====
Note: According to Microsoft if a recipient is defined in multiple policies of the same
type (anti-spam, anti-phishing, etc.), only the policy with the highest priority is applied to
the recipient. Any remaining policies of that type are not evaluated for the recipient
(including the default policy). However, it is our recommendation to audit the default
policy as well in the case a higher priority custom policy is removed. This will keep the
organization's security posture strong.
Remediation:
Note: Remediation is a two step procedure as follows:
STEP 1: Transport rules
To remediate using the UI:
1. Select Exchange to open the Exchange admin center.
2. Select Mail Flow then Rules.
3. For each rule that redirects email to external domains, select the rule and click
the 'Delete' icon.
To remediate using PowerShell:
1. Connect to Exchange Online using Connect-ExchangeOnline.
2. Run the following PowerShell command:
Remove-TransportRule {RuleName}
STEP 2: Anti-spam outbound policy
To remediate using the UI:
1. Navigate to Microsoft 365 Defender https://security.microsoft.com/
2. Expand E-mail & collaboration then select Policies & rules.
3. Select Threat policies > Anti-spam.
4. Select Anti-spam outbound policy (default)
5. Click Edit protection settings
6. Set Automatic forwarding rules dropdown to Off - Forwarding is
disabled and click Save
7. Repeat steps 4-6 for any additional higher priority, custom policies.
=====PAGE 434=====
To remediate using PowerShell:
1. Connect to Exchange Online using Connect-ExchangeOnline.
2. Run the following PowerShell command:
Set-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy -Identity {policyName} -AutoForwardingMode
Off
3. To remove AutoForwarding from all outbound policies you can also run:
Get-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy | Set-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy -
AutoForwardingMode Off
References:
1. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/exchange/security-and-compliance/mail-flow-
rules/mail-flow-rules

3. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/outbound-spam-policies-

6.2.2 Ensure mail transport rules do not whitelist specific domains
(Automated)
Profile Applicability:
• E3 Level 1
• E5 Level 1
Description:
Mail flow rules (transport rules) in Exchange Online can be configured to set the spam
confidence level (SCL) of a message to -1, which bypasses spam and phishing filtering.
When a rule applies this action to messages based on the sender's domain, all mail
from that domain is treated as trusted and skips anti-malware and anti-phishing
evaluation regardless of message content.
Rationale:
Whitelisting domains in transport rules bypasses regular malware and phishing
scanning, which can enable an attacker to launch attacks against your users from a
safe haven domain.
Note: If an organization identifies a business need for an exception, the domain should
only be whitelisted if inbound emails from that domain originate from a specific IP
address. These exceptions should be documented and regularly reviewed.
Impact:
Removing SCL bypass rules will subject previously whitelisted domains to standard
spam and phishing filtering. Mail from those domains that does not pass filtering may be
quarantined or rejected, which could disrupt established business communications.
Prior to removal, identify any rules in scope and coordinate with affected business
owners. If a legitimate need exists, consider replacing domain-based whitelisting with
approved sender lists at the connection level.
=====PAGE 436=====
Audit:
To audit using the UI:
1. Navigate to Exchange admin center https://admin.exchange.microsoft.com

content.text:
I've read both sections in your CIS M365 v7.0.0 PDF. Its audit steps answer the question, and they say something different from what we told the authors.

**6.2.1 (block mail forwarding), step 2: outbound spam policies**
- In the portal: check the Default policy, then "any additional custom outbound policies… in accordance with the organization's exclusion policies".
- In PowerShell: run `Get-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy | ft Name, AutoForwardingMode`, then "In each outbound policy verify AutoForwardingMode is Off."
- CIS adds a note: only the highest-priority policy applies to a user, but you should audit the Default policy anyway in case a custom policy is removed later.

So 6.2.1 means **every outbound policy**, whether or not any user receives it.

**2.1.15 (outbound message limits)**
- In the portal and in PowerShell, it checks only the Default policy: `Get-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy -Identity Default`.

So 2.1.15 means **the Default policy only**.

**What we decided in #2410, now on main**
- 6.2.1 checks the Default policy, plus custom policies that have an enabled rule, meaning the policies users actually receive. CodeRabbit argued for this and we agreed. It's narrower than CIS asks, because an unused custom policy that allows forwarding passes.

**How that affects the open PRs**
- **#2620** puts 6.2.1 back to checking every policy. That matches CIS exactly, and the author's new remediation is copied from the CIS remediation.
- **#2619**: our request-changes review asked the author to keep custom policies in 2.1.15, "or point to the v7 audit text that limits it to Default". That text exists, so the author was right to check Default only.

**A rule that keeps us consistent**

A CIS check should do what the benchmark's PowerShell audit step does. Where that step is broader than what users actually receive, as in 6.2.1, we stay broad. CIS tells organisations to handle exceptions through their own policy, and Maester shouldn't quietly decide that for them. Where it's narrower, as in 2.1.15, we stay narrow. Our own judgement about the policies users actually receive belongs in MT checks, not CIS ones.

The PowerShell step is the right reference because it's the automatable part of an "Automated" recommendation. It's also usually the most precise wording CIS gives.

Under that rule:
- **#2620:** keep the stricter 6.2.1, untick `restore-active-filter`, and approve once the tabs are fixed.
- **#2619:** drop our 2.1.15 point. Tell the author the v7 audit reads only the Default policy, so their change is right.

The 2.1.6 point in the same #2619 comment needs checking against its own audit text the same way.

### A requirement another suite already checks (shims)

Benchmarks overlap: CIS, CISA, ASD and Maester tests often read the same setting. Before writing a check for a
benchmark requirement, and when reviewing one:

1. **Find the tests in every suite that read the setting.** `Get-MtTest -Product <key> -Feature <key> |
   Format-Table Id, Title`, and search `tests/` for the Graph endpoint or setting name.
2. **Read the benchmark's own sources**, not only the requirement's one-line text: its audit or assessment
   guidance and any reference configuration it publishes (CIS audit and remediation sections; the SCuBA baseline
   and ScubaGear; for ASD the ISM, the Essential Eight assessment process guide and the ASD Blueprint for Secure
   Cloud). Note every concrete value: a number of days, a threshold, a role list, an authentication strength, a
   rule that must be Block. Use the web tools; cite the page.
3. **Decide:**
   - Same check: write a **shim**, a test with its own `Id`, `Title`, `Control`, `Author` and `.md` whose body is
     `return <the other test's function>` (`return Test-MtCisMfaForEveryUser`).
   - Same check, different value that the other test takes as a parameter: a shim with its own parameter whose
     default is the benchmark's value, passed on (`return Test-MtCisSmartLockoutThreshold -MaximumLockoutThreshold $MaximumLockoutThreshold`).
   - Something no test checks, or a rule no parameter covers: a check of its own. Read data through
     `internal/services/<service>/` helpers, and move a helper there (with a neutral name) when another suite
     already has the code; never copy another check's logic or name a generic helper after a suite.

A shim declares the same `Product`, `RelatedProduct`, `Feature`, `Area`, `ResourceType`, `Severity`,
`UserImpact`, `ImplementationCost`, `Mitre`, `Service`, `License`, `Permission`, `TenantType`, `Cloud`,
`Platform`, `Lifecycle`, `LongRunning` and `Exclusive` as the test it calls; calls a test that is not a shim;
passes only parameters that test declares; leaves its own requirement off that test's `Control`; and says in its
`.md` what the benchmark asks and which test it runs, by ID. `powershell/tests/general/TestShims.Tests.ps1`
enforces all of this. The full guidance, with an example, is
[Tests that another suite already has](../../../website/docs/writing-tests/index.mdx#tests-that-another-suite-already-has).

When reviewing, fail a benchmark check that re-implements a check another suite already has when the benchmark's
sources give no reason for the difference, and say which test it duplicates and which source you read.

## Validation Checklist

### Test logic
- [ ] Returns exactly one `$true`/`$false`; no stray pipeline output.
- [ ] No other suite already checks the same setting; or the benchmark's own sources were read and the check is
      a shim of that test, or differs from it for a reason those sources give.
- [ ] No `Test-MtConnection` guard, no `Get-MtLicenseInformation` check; `Service` and `License` declared instead.
- [ ] No blanket `try { } catch { Add-MtTestResultDetail -SkippedBecause Error ... }`.
- [ ] `-SkippedBecause NotApplicable` (not `$null`) when the check does not apply.
- [ ] Data retrieval uses `Invoke-MtGraphRequest` or Maester helpers.
- [ ] No hard-coded GUIDs, tenant IDs or names; tunables are described parameters.
- [ ] No writes to `$script:`, `$global:`, `$env:` or `$__MtSession`.
- [ ] `Platform = 'Windows'` if it uses Windows-only commands.

### Attribute and files
- [ ] `Test.<Id>.ps1` and `Test.<Id>.md` in the right suite folder; ID unique and not reused.

## Tests that another suite already has

Benchmarks overlap. CIS, CISA SCuBA and ASD all ask for multifactor authentication for every user, and Maester
has its own test for it as well. Before you write a test for a benchmark requirement, look for a test that
already reads the same setting, then decide from the benchmark's own sources whether it asks for anything that
test does not check.

1. **Find the tests that read the setting.** `Get-MtTest -Product entra -Feature conditional-access | Format-Table
   Id, Title` lists the candidates; searching `tests/` for the Graph endpoint or the setting name finds the rest.
   Look in every suite, not only the one you are writing for.
2. **Read what the benchmark asks, in its own sources.** The one-line text of a requirement is usually generic.
   The detail that decides between two implementations is in the benchmark's audit or assessment guidance and in
   any reference configuration it publishes: the audit and remediation sections of a CIS benchmark, the SCuBA
   baseline and ScubaGear for CISA, and for ASD the ISM, the Essential Eight assessment process guide and the ASD
   Blueprint for Secure Cloud. Note every concrete value they name: a number of days, a threshold, a list of
   roles, an authentication strength, a rule that must be set to Block.
3. **Choose what to write:**

| What the benchmark asks | What you write |
| --- | --- |
| What an existing test checks | A shim: a test with its own ID, title, `Control` and guide whose body returns the result of the existing test |
| The same check with a different value, which the existing test takes as a parameter | A shim that passes the value, with the benchmark's value as the default of its own parameter |
| Something no test checks, or a rule no parameter covers | A test of its own. Read the data with the helpers in `powershell/internal/services/<service>/`, and move a helper there when another suite has the code you need; don't copy another test's logic |

## What a benchmark test evaluates

A CIS test does what the benchmark's **PowerShell audit procedure** does: it reads the same objects and passes on
the same condition. The PowerShell steps are the part of an Automated recommendation that can be automated, and
usually its most precise wording. When the UI steps and the PowerShell steps differ, follow the PowerShell steps.

- **Scope.** When the audit reads every object, the test reads every object, including ones that apply to no
  user. CIS 6.2.1 runs `Get-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy` and checks `AutoForwardingMode` on each policy, so
  the test checks custom policies that have no rule. When the audit reads one object, the test reads only that
  one: CIS 2.1.15 runs `Get-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy -Identity Default`, so the test does not evaluate
  custom policies. Don't narrow a test to the policies users receive, or widen it beyond what the audit reads.
  CIS leaves exceptions to the organization, so a test does not decide them for it.
- **Values.** Use the thresholds the audit names or its script sets, such as the 90% of the extension list in
  CIS 2.1.11. When organizations may need a different value, make it a parameter with the benchmark's value as
  its default.
- **Missing data.** When the object the audit reads is not returned, the test fails or reports an error. It never
  passes because there was nothing to check.

A view of the policies users actually receive belongs in a Maester (MT) test, not in a benchmark test. The same
rule applies to CISA tests, with the SCuBA baseline and ScubaGear's policy in place of the CIS audit procedure.

﻿function Get-MtAffectedObjectFromCache {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Derives the affected objects from the request caches in the current Maester session.

    .DESCRIPTION
    Walks $__MtSession.GraphCache and $__MtSession.GitHubCache — both keyed by request URL —
    and parses each key into a normalized object record (System / AnchorKind / Type / Id / SourceUri).

    Graph URIs yield:
    - Instance records when a path segment is a GUID (e.g. users/{id}/authentication/methods)
      or a quoted key (e.g. authenticationMethodConfigurations('Fido2'))
    - Singleton records for tenant-level config resources (e.g. policies/authorizationPolicy)
    - Collection records for plain collection reads (e.g. users, servicePrincipals)

    GitHub cache keys ({ApiVersion}|{AbsoluteUri}) yield External records for the
    organization or repository addressed by the request.

    This is a run-level view (what data the run touched), not per-test attribution.
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([object[]])]
    param()

    $guidPattern = '^[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-([0-9a-fA-F]{4}-){3}[0-9a-fA-F]{12}$'
    # Graph resources that are always tenant-level singletons when read without a key
    $singletonPrefixes = @(
        'policies', 'settings', 'organization', 'admin', 'identityProtection/settings',
        'reports', 'directory/recommendations', 'networkAccess'
    )
    # Graph collections whose keyed reads address a directory object the rest of the inventory
    # already knows under a canonical EntraID type. Mapping them here means a check that both
    # reads users/{id} and renders a portal link produces one object, not two.
    # applications is deliberately absent: the cache keys it by object id while the portal links
    # parsed from markdown carry the app id, so the two would not merge anyway.
    $directoryTypes = @{
        users             = 'User'
        groups            = 'Group'
        devices           = 'Device'
        servicePrincipals = 'ServicePrincipal'
        directoryRoles    = 'DirectoryRole'
    }

    # Keyed reads below these collections address an object the checks also link to under a
    # canonical type, so the read merges with it instead of listing it a second time as a Graph path:
    # accessPackages/{id}/accessPackageResourceRoleScopes is that access package.
    $keyedObjectTypes = @{
        'identityGovernance/entitlementManagement/accessPackages'        = 'AccessPackage'
        'identityGovernance/entitlementManagement/accessPackageCatalogs' = 'AccessPackageCatalog'
    }

    # Action endpoints are verbs, not resources: they address no object worth inventorying.
    $actionSegments = @('$batch', 'runHuntingQuery', 'getMemberGroups', 'getMemberObjects', 'checkMemberGroups')

    $records = [System.Collections.Generic.List[object]]::new()

    if ($__MtSession.GraphCache) {
        foreach ($key in $__MtSession.GraphCache.Keys) {
            # POST cache keys append "_<json body>" (or a bare "_" when the body is empty). A plain
            # underscore is part of the path: guest UPNs look like john_contoso.com#EXT#@tenant.
            $uri = ($key -split '_(?=[\{\[]|$)', 2)[0]
            if ($uri -notmatch '^https://[^/]*graph[^/]*/(v1\.0|beta)/(.+)$') { continue }
            $path = $Matches[2]
            # Strip query string
            $path = ($path -split '\?', 2)[0].TrimEnd('/')
            if ([string]::IsNullOrEmpty($path)) { continue }

            $segments = $path -split '/'
            if ($segments[-1] -in $actionSegments) { continue }

            # A keyed read of a directory collection is the object itself, whatever sub-resource
            # follows: users/{id}/authentication/methods is still that user, not a fifth object.
            # The key may be a GUID or a UPN, and a UPN must be recognised or it lands in Type,
            # where the report's PII redaction never reaches it.
            if ($segments.Count -ge 2 -and $directoryTypes.ContainsKey($segments[0])) {
                # Cache keys are AbsoluteUri values, so a UPN arrives percent-encoded (#EXT# as %23EXT%23).
                $directoryKey = [uri]::UnescapeDataString($segments[1])
            } else {
                $directoryKey = $null

Review target: `2625`

`high effort → 8 inline angles → dedup (no verify) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle + 1 conventions angle, up to 6 each)

Run **8 independent finder angles** in sequence yourself, in THIS context — do NOT spawn subagents for them. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

### Conventions (CLAUDE.md)

Find the CLAUDE.md files that govern the changed code: the user-level
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the repo-root CLAUDE.md, plus any CLAUDE.md or
CLAUDE.local.md in a directory that is an ancestor of a changed file (a
directory's CLAUDE.md only applies to files at or below it). Read each one
that exists, then check the diff for clear violations of the rules they state.

Only flag a violation when you can quote the exact rule and the exact line
that breaks it — no style preferences, no vague "spirit of the doc"
inferences. In the finding, name the CLAUDE.md path and quote the rule so the
report can cite it. If no CLAUDE.md applies, return nothing for this angle.

Cleanup, altitude, and conventions candidates use the same
`file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in `failure_scenario`, state the concrete
cost (what is duplicated, wasted, harder to maintain, or which CLAUDE.md rule
is broken) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank cleanup,
altitude, and conventions findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates are the dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Dedup only (no verify)

Pool all candidates. Dedup near-duplicates only (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). Do NOT run verifiers; do NOT re-judge. Sort by severity.

## Output

Target **at least 5 findings**. If fewer genuine findings exist, emit what you have — do not invent to hit the floor.

Call the ReportFindings tool once to report this review's results
with `{level, findings}`. `findings` is at most 10 entries ranked
most-severe first; each entry has `file`, `line`, `summary`,
`short_summary` — the claim compressed to ≤60 characters, no rationale
or consequence clause — `failure_scenario`, and `category` — a short kebab-case slug for the angle
that produced it (`correctness`, `simplification`, `efficiency`,

findings.short_summary: Non-404 group errors may now break GDAP/MSP tenants
findings.summary: Every non-404 error reading a group now throws, but the old code skipped all such errors with a warning, and nothing confirms that external GDAP partner groups or other unreadable groups surface as 404 rather than 400 or 403.
findings.failure_scenario: An MSP-managed tenant has a role assigned to a group that `groups/{id}/` answers with 403 Authorization_RequestDenied or 400 Invalid object identifier rather than 404. CIS 1.1.1 and 1.1.3, CISA MS.AAD.7.x, MT.1020 and every `Get-MtPrivilegedRoleUser` caller then report Error on every run, where they used to evaluate the remaining members.

findings.summary: The fallback `$ErrorRecord.Exception.Message -match 'NotFound|404'` is unanchored, so any message containing "404" (an object id, a Retry-After value, a URL) is treated as not found and silently skipped.
findings.failure_scenario: A 403 or 429 whose message includes a group id like `...4048-...` or `retry after 404 ms` matches the regex. `Get-MtGroupMember` returns $null, and the check passes without the group's members: the false pass this PR is meant to remove.

findings.short_summary: String throw discards the original ErrorRecord/status
findings.summary: `throw "Could not read group ...: $($_.Exception.Message)"` replaces the HttpResponseException with a plain RuntimeException, so callers lose the status code and the inner exception.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller or the engine that wants to treat 429/throttling differently from 403, or log the Graph request id, gets only a string. `Test-MtGraphNotFoundError` on the rethrown error from a nested group can only match the message text, which compounds the regex problem above.

findings.short_summary: Hashtable responses now cached under a type-blind key
findings.summary: Removing -DisableCache means MT.1024 and MT.1059 now store `-OutputType Hashtable` responses in the Graph cache, whose key ignores OutputType (the CodeRabbit finding).
findings.failure_scenario: A custom test or pack reads `directory/recommendations?$expand=impactedResources` or `security/identities/healthIssues` with the default PSObject output after MT.1024 or MT.1059 has run, and gets the cached Hashtable. The reverse order gives MT.1024 a PSObject. Property access or `Format-Result` then behaves differently and can report no instances.

findings.short_summary: MT.1059 mutates the now-cached response objects
findings.summary: With the cache on, MT.1059's `Add-Member` calls and its assignments to `severity`/`status` (title-casing them) change the objects stored in `$__MtSession.GraphCache`, not a private copy.
findings.failure_scenario: Any later reader of `security/identities/healthIssues` in the same session, such as a family instance, a custom test or the affected-objects report, sees the title-cased severity and the injected `domainNamesString`/`sensorDNSNamesString` properties instead of Graph's data.

findings.summary: The test only looks for the token `DisableCache`, so other ways to bypass the cache pass. Examples: `Get-MtSpo -ClearCache`, `Clear-MtGraphCache` inside a check, `-NoCache $true` on internal helpers, and `-DisableCache:$true` from an allow-listed file (the bare-switch check only catches a switch with no argument).
findings.failure_scenario: A new check calls `Get-MtSpo -ClearCache` or `Clear-MtGraphCache`, or an allow-listed helper writes `-DisableCache:$true`. The unit test still passes, although the AGENTS.md rule and the CodeRabbit instruction say these are not allowed.

findings.short_summary: Public Get-MtRoleMember now returns session-stale data
findings.summary: `Get-MtRoleMember` is public and interactive users call it. Removing -DisableCache means repeated calls in one session return the first result until `Clear-MtGraphCache`, and neither the help nor the PR description says so.
findings.failure_scenario: An admin runs `Get-MtRoleMember -Role GlobalAdministrator`, removes an assignment in the portal and runs it again in the same session: the removed admin still appears. Neither the help nor the release notes mention that this changed.

findings.short_summary: Extra GET groups/{id} before reading members
findings.summary: `Get-MtGroupMember` still reads `groups/{id}/` first, only to log `displayName`. Now that both reads use the same 404/throw handling, the members request alone is enough.
findings.failure_scenario: Every role-assigned or forwarding-profile group costs two Graph requests instead of one. That doubles calls and throttling exposure on large tenants and in recursive expansion, with no change in behaviour.

content.text:
I've made the #2619 and #2620 fixes myself, and their cards now hold approval drafts for you to queue. The CIS rule is in its own PR. CI is still running on both contributor branches.

**#2620:** I pushed `d568f1e` to the author's branch, replacing the tabs in the 6.1.2 script with spaces.
- **Tests:** they passed, apart from the ZeroTrustAssessment test that always fails on your Mac. One more failure was the stale `test-builder.json` from before #2622; the branch hasn't picked up that fix from main yet.
- **Draft approval:** keeps the stricter 6.2.1, because the CIS audit checks every outbound policy. It also thanks the author for the remediation and for listing the behaviour changes, and points to #2626.

**#2619:** I pushed `cc89d3f`, so 2.1.12 and 2.1.13 now fail with "compliance could not be established" when no Default connection filter policy comes back, instead of passing.
- **Tests:** only the ZeroTrustAssessment failure.
- **Draft approval:** under the new rule, most of our earlier review falls away, and the draft says so point by point:
  - **2.1.15:** the audit reads Default only, so the author's change is right.
  - **2.1.6:** following custom policies matches the audit's note about the highest-priority policy.
  - **2.1.11:** the 90% threshold comes from the CIS audit script, and rules were already matched on Id, Name and Identity.
  - **2.1.7:** the audit reads only `AntiPhishRule`, so our preset point doesn't apply.
  - **2.1.4 and 2.1.7 scope:** the audit asks for a judgement call here.
- **Still to clear:** our earlier request for changes on #2619 stays in place until you queue the approval.

**[#2626](https://github.com/maester365/maester/pull/2626), the CIS rule:** a CIS test does what the benchmark's PowerShell audit does, in three ways:
- **Scope:** it reads the same objects.
- **Values:** it uses the same thresholds.
- **Missing data:** it fails or errors when the audited object is missing, and never passes.

The rule is now in:
- the writing-tests guide, as "What a benchmark test evaluates";
- the test-expert skill, including its review checklist;
- `.coderabbit.yaml`, for `tests/cis` and `tests/cisa`.

#2625 and #2626 both edit the same spot in `.coderabbit.yaml`, so whichever merges second will need that one-line conflict fixed.

**PR Desk skill:** it now records three rulings:
- the CIS audit rule, with the PDF to read;
- make small fixes ourselves when the PR allows it;
- describe fixes we've already pushed in the comment, rather than listing them as fixes to tick.

The search didn't return anything that addresses the specific question about `roleAssignments`, `$expand=principal`, or foreign security groups. It returned only the overview page for the GDAP API, in several languages.

The overview does cover a few relevant points:

- GDAP gives partners least-privileged access to their customer tenants following the Zero Trust cybersecurity model, and customers have to explicitly grant that access.
- To enable admin on behalf of (AOBO) access to a customer tenant, the workflow ends by creating a new access assignment for the delegated admin relationship by using the Create accessAssignments API.
- On permissions, the page notes that the calling principal must be in the partner tenant and be granted the appropriate granular delegated admin privileges permissions. This is the closest result to your principal question, but it does not mention security groups or expansion.

The results do not explain how group principals in a customer tenant are resolved through `roleAssignments` or `$expand=principal`. I've pushed `5e1dc33` to #2625, fixing seven of the eight review findings, and resolved both code-scanning comments. The full unit test suite passed, apart from the usual ZeroTrustAssessment failure.

**Review fixes:**
- **404 check:** `Test-MtGraphNotFoundError` now reads the status code from the error and the error wrapped inside it. It only falls back to the message for `Request_ResourceNotFound` or a "Not Found" status. A stray "404" inside an object id or retry delay no longer counts, which I checked against six sample errors.
- **Error kept:** `Get-MtGroupMember` throws an error that keeps the Graph exception inside, so its status code can still be read.
  - It uses `throw`, not `$PSCmdlet.ThrowTerminatingError`. The second only stops the caller's current line, so `Get-MtRoleMember` would have carried on with no members, which is the same false pass we're removing.
  - A new test checks that the calling script stops.
- **One request per group:** `Get-MtGroupMember` no longer reads the group itself before its members.
- **Cache key:** a `Hashtable` response is now cached under its own key (`…_[Hashtable]`), so a default caller never gets one. The affected-objects report already strips that suffix, and a test confirms it.
- **MT.1059** works on copies of the cached health issues instead of changing them. A new test fails without this fix.
- **Cache guard test** now also catches:
  - `NoCache` and `ClearCache`;
  - calls to the `Clear-Mt*Cache` commands;
  - `-DisableCache:$true`;
  - checks that reset `$__MtSession` caches.

  I planted each of these in throwaway files, and the test caught every one. Disconnecting and resetting the module are allowed to clear caches.
- **`Get-MtRoleMember` help** now says results come from the session cache, and to run `Clear-MtGraphCache` to read them again.
- **Not fixed: GDAP groups.** I couldn't confirm how Graph answers for a partner's group without a GDAP tenant. Graph normally returns 404 for an object id that isn't in the tenant, so these groups should still be skipped, but that's untested.

**Code scanning:** the only two warnings from this PR were PSScriptAnalyzer flagging my test helper `New-HttpError`. I renamed it to `Get-HttpError`, replied on both threads and resolved them. The other open alerts are in files this PR doesn't touch, such as `LdapPaging.Tests.ps1`.

input.recap: I pushed 3f20318 to #2625, which fixes the status-code cast and catches indexed writes to the session cache. I replied to and resolved all seven CodeRabbit threads: I took two suggestions and declined three. The full unit test suite passes apart from the usual ZeroTrustAssessment failure.

content.text:
I pushed `3f20318` to #2625, and all seven CodeRabbit threads are now answered and resolved. I'd count about half of CodeRabbit's comments on this PR as overboard. The full unit test suite passes, apart from the usual ZeroTrustAssessment failure.

**How we solved the cache key comment (your screenshot):** we fixed it in `5e1dc33`. When a caller asks `Invoke-MtGraphRequest` for any output type other than the default (PSObject), the result is cached under its own key, with `_[Hashtable]` added. So a Hashtable read and a PSObject read of the same URL can't hand each other the wrong shape.
- Default callers keep exactly the keys they had before.
- The affected-objects report removes the suffix before it reads the key.
- Tests cover both.

**Callers that ask for a different output type:** only seven calls do this, and all ask for Hashtable:
- MT.1024 (`directory/recommendations`);
- MT.1059 (`security/identities/healthIssues`);
- five calls in `Get-MtUser` (role members, emergency access user and group, users with a filter).

None of them reads the same URL with the same `$select` as a default caller. The bug CodeRabbit described couldn't happen with today's code, and the suffix keeps it from happening in future. A few files call `Invoke-MgGraphRequest` directly with `-OutputType`, but those calls skip our cache altogether, so they aren't affected.

**Rechecking all the review comments:**

| Comment | Verdict |
|---|---|
| A "404" inside an id counted as not found (earlier) | Valid. That would be a false pass, which is what this PR removes. Fixed in `5e1dc33`. |
| Include the output type in the cache key (earlier) | Correct in principle, but it couldn't happen today, and CodeRabbit labelled it "Major". The fix was cheap. Fixed in `5e1dc33`. |
| The `[int]` cast throws on a text status code | Valid. The cast failure would replace the real Graph error. Fixed, with new tests. |
| Indexed writes to the session cache aren't caught (nitpick) | Valid, and that's the most likely way code would write to the cache. Fixed. |
| Detect quoted `'DisableCache'` keys in splatted hashtables | Overboard. The test already catches unquoted keys, and a quoted one would only get through on purpose. Declined. |
| Allow the bare `-DisableCache` only on one line of `Invoke-MtGraphRequest` (earlier nitpick) | Overboard. That file is the transport itself, and the proposed check matches the line's exact text, so it breaks on any reformat. Declined. |
| Add an exception for batched requests to the cache rule in `.coderabbit.yaml` | The fact is right: batched `$batch` reads aren't cached. But writing the exception into the rule would weaken it. Declined. |

The batch point is the one real gap left. A check that reads several IDs in one batched call goes to Graph every time, so two checks can see different data within a run. The fix is to cache each item in a batch under its own key. That's separate work, and no check has broken because of it so far.

function Get-MtEntraRecommendationInstance {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Returns one MT.1024 instance per Entra recommendation of the tenant.

    .DESCRIPTION
    Instance source of the MT.1024 family. The suffix is the recommendation ID without its tenant prefix
    (MT.1024.<recommendation>), the title is the recommendation's display name and the severity its
    priority in title case, as the Maester 2.x rows showed them.
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([pscustomobject])]
    param()

    $response = Invoke-MtGraphRequest -DisableCache -ApiVersion beta -RelativeUri 'directory/recommendations?$expand=impactedResources' -OutputType Hashtable
    $textInfo = (Get-Culture).TextInfo
    foreach ($recommendation in @($response.value)) {
        if ($null -eq $recommendation) { continue }
        [pscustomobject]@{
            Id       = $recommendation.id -replace '^[^_]+_', ''
            Title    = "$($recommendation.displayName)."
            Severity = $textInfo.ToTitleCase([string]$recommendation.priority)
            Tag      = @($recommendation.recommendationType | Where-Object { $_ })
            Data     = $recommendation
        }
    }
}

content.text:
Today's run didn't test the `Invoke-MtGraphRequest` change. You imported the module from `~/github/maester`, which is on `feat/console-status-pill`. That branch was last committed on 28 Oct at 18:26, the same minute your earlier run finished. It's 175 commits behind main and doesn't contain #2625. For example, MT.1024 in that checkout still passes `-DisableCache`, and there's no output-type cache key. So both runs used the same code.

**The two runs match.** All 859 tests have the same result in both. Six tests worded their details differently, and none of that comes from the code:
- **MT.1092, MT.1197, MT.1234:** a date or "days remaining" moved on.
- **MT.1032:** the same four Global Admins, listed in a different order.
- **MT.1022:** "P1 licenses utilized" went from 1 to 0, which is the tenant's own licence data.
- **MT.1024.staleApps:** the Zero Trust Assessment app went from Fail to Pass. Entra's recommendation data changed; the code didn't.

**To test the change fairly**, compare #2625 with the main commit it was built on, not with 28 Oct. Since then main has gained other changes that would muddy the comparison, such as the CIS fixes in #2619 and #2620. I set up two checkouts:
- `~/github/maester-baseline`: main at `9c520df`, the exact commit merged into #2625.
- `~/github/maester-pr2625`: #2625 at `d0e2171`.

Run these in a fresh PowerShell session for each one, so the module doesn't carry over:

```bash
cd ~/github/maester-baseline && pwsh -NoProfile -c 'Import-Module ./powershell/Maester.psd1 -Force; Connect-Maester; Invoke-Maester -OutputFolder ~/github/maester/test-results -OutputFolderFileName elapora-baseline'
```

```bash
cd ~/github/maester-pr2625 && pwsh -NoProfile -c 'Import-Module ./powershell/Maester.psd1 -Force; Connect-Maester; Invoke-Maester -OutputFolder ~/github/maester/test-results -OutputFolderFileName elapora-pr2625'
```

Once both have finished, I'll compare results, details and errors test by test. I'll pay particular attention to the 13 checks that no longer bypass the cache, MT.1024 and MT.1059 (the Hashtable callers), the `Get-MtRoleMember` checks, and the run time.
can i run them in parallel in two different console sesions

Yes, you can run them at the same time. Each console is its own PowerShell process, so the two copies of the module and their session caches stay separate. Neither run can read the other's cached Graph responses. The output files have different names, so they won't overwrite each other, and both sign-ins share the same token cache without trouble.

Running them together has two costs:

- **Throttling:** two full runs at once double the load on the tenant. If Graph or Exchange start returning 429s, one run may wait and retry, or record an error the other run doesn't. That would show up as a difference that has nothing to do with the code. If you see one, I'll check whether it was throttling before blaming the change.
- **Timing:** the two runs slow each other down, so comparing their durations tells us nothing. The change to the cache should mean fewer Graph calls, so if you want to measure that speed-up, run them one after the other.

If you only want to know whether anything broke, run them in parallel. If you also want to know whether it got faster, run them in sequence.

        Title = 'Privileged access to systems and their resources is disabled after 45 days of inactivity.',
        Product = 'entra',
        Feature = 'roles',
        Area = 'privileged-access',
        ResourceType = 'User',
        Severity = 'Medium',
        UserImpact = 'Low',
        ImplementationCost = 'Medium',
        Mitre = 'T1078.004',
        Control = ('essential-eight:ISM-1648', 'nist-800-53-r5:AC-2(3)'),
        Service = 'Graph',
        License = 'AAD_PREMIUM',
        Author = 'jusso-dev'
    )]
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([bool])]
    param(
        # Days without a sign-in after which privileged access must be disabled.
        [ValidateRange(1, 365)]
        [int] $InactiveDays = 45
    )

    $rolesOf = Get-MtPrivilegedRoleUser -ExcludeEmergencyAccessAccount
    if ($rolesOf.Count -eq 0) {
        Add-MtTestResultDetail -SkippedBecause NotApplicable
        return $null
    }

    $cutoff = [datetime]::UtcNow.AddDays(-$InactiveDays)
    $users = @(Invoke-MtGraphRequest -RelativeUri 'users' -UniqueId @($rolesOf.Keys) -Select id, userPrincipalName, displayName, accountEnabled, createdDateTime, signInActivity)
    $inactive = foreach ($user in $users) {
        if ($user.accountEnabled -ne $true) { continue }
        $signIns = @($user.signInActivity.lastSignInDateTime, $user.signInActivity.lastNonInteractiveSignInDateTime | Where-Object { $_ } | ForEach-Object { [datetime]$_ })
        $lastSignIn = if ($signIns.Count -gt 0) { ($signIns | Measure-Object -Maximum).Maximum.ToUniversalTime() } else { $null }
        $isInactive = if ($lastSignIn) { $lastSignIn -lt $cutoff } else { $user.createdDateTime -and ([datetime]$user.createdDateTime).ToUniversalTime() -lt $cutoff }
        if ($isInactive) {
            [pscustomobject]@{
                id                = $user.id
                displayName       = $user.displayName
                userPrincipalName = $user.userPrincipalName
                LastSignIn        = if ($lastSignIn) { $lastSignIn.ToString('yyyy-MM-dd') } else { 'Never' }
                Roles             = $rolesOf[$user.id] -join ', '
            }
        }
    }
    $inactive = @($inactive)
    $testResult = $inactive.Count -eq 0

    if ($testResult) {
        $testResultMarkdown = "Well done. Every enabled user with a privileged directory role signed in within the last $InactiveDays days ($($rolesOf.Count) users checked)."
    } else {
        $table = "| User | Last sign-in | Privileged roles |`n| --- | --- | --- |`n"
        foreach ($user in ($inactive | Sort-Object userPrincipalName)) { $table += "| $($user.userPrincipalName) | $($user.LastSignIn) | $($user.Roles) |`n" }
        $testResultMarkdown = "$($inactive.Count) enabled user(s) with a privileged directory role have not signed in for $InactiveDays days or more. Disable the account or remove the role, and let an access review or a PIM alert catch the next one.`n`n$table"
    }
    Add-MtTestResultDetail -Result $testResultMarkdown
    return $testResult

content.text:
The #2625 change doesn't appear to have broken anything. All 909 results match between the main baseline and #2625. One check, ASD.ISM-1648, listed fewer users on #2625, and I think that comes from a bug already on main, not from #2625. I haven't confirmed that yet.

| | Main (`9c520df`) | #2625 (`d0e2171`) |
|---|---|---|
| Passed / Failed / Investigate | 150 / 174 / 1 | 150 / 174 / 1 |
| Skipped / Error / Not run | 265 / 0 / 319 | 265 / 0 / 319 |
| Duration | 4:54 | 4:32 |

The duration doesn't tell us much, because the two runs slowed each other down.

**What matches:** every test has the same result and the same skip reason. The checks this PR touched report exactly the same details on both branches:
- the 13 checks that no longer bypass the cache;
- MT.1024 and MT.1059, which ask for Hashtable output;
- the checks that read role members through `Get-MtRoleMember`.

**Differences that don't matter:**
- **Skipped tests (57):** their error records differ only in the checkout folder path in the stack trace.
- **MT.1092:** an `id` in the Intune payload changes on every call, even between two runs of the same code.
- **MT.1178:** the same rows, listed in a different order.

**The one that matters: ASD.ISM-1648** found 9 inactive privileged users on main and 6 on #2625. The three missing users are AdeleV, annaj and MeganB.

- This check reads users with one batched Graph call that includes `signInActivity`, a property Microsoft throttles heavily. Batched calls aren't cached, and #2625 didn't change how they work.
- `Invoke-MtGraphRequest` passes on whatever each item in the batch returns. If an item fails, for example with a 429 when throttled, the check gets an error object instead of a user. That object has no `accountEnabled`, so the check skips it without any warning.
- Your two parallel runs doubled the load on the tenant, which makes a 429 likely. If that's what happened, it fits exactly: three users vanished silently, and the check still passed or failed as normal.

To confirm it, run ASD.ISM-1648 on its own in the #2625 checkout. If it lists 9 users, throttling was the cause:

```bash
cd ~/github/maester-pr2625 && pwsh -NoProfile -c 'Import-Module ./powershell/Maester.psd1 -Force; Connect-Maester; Invoke-Maester -TestId ASD.ISM-1648 -OutputFolder ~/github/maester/test-results -OutputFolderFileName elapora-ism1648'
```

Whichever way that goes, the batch handling is a real false-pass risk for any check that reads objects in a batch. A throttled read can make users disappear from a report. The fix would retry 429s after the wait Graph asks for, keep skipping objects that return 404 as it does today, and raise an error for anything else. I'd put that in its own PR off main. I've kept `~/github/maester-baseline` and `~/github/maester-pr2625` in case you want to run more tests.

﻿function Invoke-MtGraphRequest {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Enhanced version of Invoke-MgGraphRequest that supports paging, batching and caching.

    .Description
    The version of Invoke-Graph request supports
    * Filter, Select and Unique IDs as parameters
    * Automatic paging if Graph returns a nextLink
    * Batching of requests to Graph if multiple requests are piped through
    * Caching of results for the duration of the session
    * Ability to skip cache and go directly to Graph
    * Specify consistency level as a parameter

    :::info
    Note: Batch requests don't support caching.
    :::

    .Example
    Invoke-MtGraph -RelativeUri "users" -Filter "displayName eq 'John Doe'" -Select "displayName"

    Get all users with a display name of "John Doe" and return the first 10 results.

    .LINK
    https://maester.dev/docs/commands/Invoke-MtGraphRequest
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        # Graph endpoint such as "users".
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true, Position = 0, ValueFromPipeline = $true)]
        [string[]] $RelativeUri,
        # Specifies unique Id(s) for the URI endpoint. For example, users endpoint accepts Id or UPN.
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [string[]] $UniqueId,
        # Filters properties (columns).
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [string[]] $Select,
        # Filters results (rows). https://docs.microsoft.com/graph/query-parameters#filter-parameter
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [string] $Filter,
        # Parameters such as "$top".
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [hashtable] $QueryParameters,
        # API Version.
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [ValidateSet('v1.0', 'beta')]
        [string] $ApiVersion = 'v1.0',
        # HTTP Method to use for the request.
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [ValidateSet('GET', 'POST')]
        [string] $Method = 'GET',
        # Body for POST requests.
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [string] $Body,
        # Specifies consistency level.
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [string] $ConsistencyLevel = 'eventual',
        # Only return first page of results.
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [switch] $DisablePaging,
        # Force individual requests to MS Graph.
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [switch] $DisableBatching,
        # Specify Batch size.
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [int] $BatchSize = 20,
        # Base URL for Microsoft Graph API.
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [uri] $GraphBaseUri,
        # Specify if this request should skip cache and go directly to Graph.
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [switch] $DisableCache,
        # Specify the output type
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [ValidateSet('PSObject', 'PSCustomObject', 'Hashtable')]
        [string] $OutputType = 'PSObject'
    )

    begin {
        # An explicit -GraphBaseUri is an intentional absolute endpoint override. Without one the
        # endpoint is read from the active Graph context on every invocation, so a context switch
        # inside a single session is picked up instead of reusing a stale session value.
        [bool] $IsEndpointOverride = -not [string]::IsNullOrEmpty($GraphBaseUri)
        if (!$IsEndpointOverride) {
            $MgContext = Get-MgContext
            if (-not $MgContext -or [string]::IsNullOrEmpty($MgContext.Environment)) {
                throw "No active Microsoft Graph context. Ensure you are connected via 'Connect-Maester', or pass -GraphBaseUri to target an endpoint explicitly."
            }
            # Resolved on every invocation, not memoised. Memoising by environment name misses
            # an endpoint changed under that same name by Add-MgEnvironment or
            # Set-MgEnvironment, and the stale endpoint would then also produce the absolute
            # cache key, so a request could be answered from the previous endpoint's entry.
            # Measured cost of not caching it: Get-MgEnvironment is 0.031 ms per call against
            # a Graph round trip of tens of milliseconds.
            [string] $EnvironmentName = $MgContext.Environment
            Write-Verbose -Message ("Resolving the Graph endpoint for environment '{0}'." -f $EnvironmentName)
            # Get-MgEnvironment answers an unknown name with $null and writes no error
            # (measured against Microsoft.Graph.Authentication 2.41.2), so an environment the
            # SDK does not know leaves $GraphBaseUri null and surfaces four lines later as
            # "You cannot call a method on a null-valued expression" -- a message that names
            # neither the environment nor the cause. Refuse here, where the name is still in
            # hand. An environment registered with Add-MgEnvironment but given no
            # GraphEndpoint fails the same way and is caught by the same check.
            $ResolvedEndpoint = (Get-MgEnvironment -Name $EnvironmentName -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).GraphEndpoint
            if ([string]::IsNullOrEmpty($ResolvedEndpoint)) {
                throw "The Microsoft Graph environment '$EnvironmentName' has no known Graph endpoint. Check the environment name with 'Get-MgEnvironment', or pass -GraphBaseUri to target an endpoint explicitly."
            }
            $GraphBaseUri = [uri] $ResolvedEndpoint
        }
        # Exposed for callers that read the session value; no longer used to route requests.
        $__MtSession.GraphBaseUri = $GraphBaseUri

        # The endpoint itself can carry a path, for example a reverse proxy in front of Graph. A base
        # that does not end in a slash makes its last segment look like a document, which would put
        # that segment back into any uri made relative to it. Normalising the base once, here, is what
        # keeps the rest of this function from having to care whether the endpoint has a path.
        [uri] $TransportBaseUri = [uri] ($GraphBaseUri.AbsoluteUri.TrimEnd('/') + '/')

        # Whether a relative transport uri is safe for THIS endpoint. Measured against
        # Microsoft.Graph.Authentication 2.41.2 by calling InvokeMgGraphRequest.PrepareUri
        # directly: it builds a relative request from the base address's scheme and host only,
        # so both the endpoint's own path and an explicit port are dropped.
        #
        #   base https://graph.microsoft.com/          + v1.0/users -> https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users
        #   base https://proxy.contoso.com/graph/      + v1.0/users -> https://proxy.contoso.com/v1.0/users
        #   base https://proxy.contoso.com:8443/graph/ + v1.0/users -> https://proxy.contoso.com/v1.0/users
        #
        # A relative uri is therefore only equivalent when the endpoint is a bare host on the
        # default port, which every published Microsoft cloud is. Anything else -- a reverse
        # proxy with a path, a non-default port -- goes out absolute, where nothing is dropped.
        [bool] $RelativeIsSafe = ($TransportBaseUri.AbsolutePath -eq '/') -and $TransportBaseUri.IsDefaultPort

        # Versioned root that every uri in this invocation is built from. Batch subrequest urls are
        # relative to it, so the base and the api version come off together and a base uri that
        # carries a path of its own does not leak into the subrequest. Built through UriBuilder so
        # it is normalised exactly like the request uris it is compared against.
        [string] $VersionedBaseUri = (New-Object System.UriBuilder -ArgumentList ($TransportBaseUri.AbsoluteUri + $ApiVersion)).Uri.AbsoluteUri.TrimEnd('/') + '/'

        $listRequests = New-Object 'System.Collections.Generic.List[psobject]'

        # The override-versus-relative decision lives here only, so the single-request path and the
        # batch path cannot drift apart. Relative by default is what lets Microsoft Graph PowerShell
        # route to the connected environment; absolute only when the caller overrode the endpoint.
        function Resolve-TransportUri ([uri] $RequestUri) {
            if ($IsEndpointOverride -or -not $RelativeIsSafe) { return $RequestUri.AbsoluteUri }
            return $TransportBaseUri.MakeRelativeUri($RequestUri).ToString()
        }

        function Format-Result ($results, $RawOutput) {
            # Check if 'value' property exists (not just truthy) to handle empty arrays
            $hasValueProperty = $null -ne $results -and $results.PSObject.Properties.Match('value').Count -gt 0
            if (!$RawOutput -and $hasValueProperty) {
                $dataContextName = '@odata.context'
                foreach ($result in $results.value) {
                    if ($result -is [hashtable]) {
                        if (!$result.ContainsKey($dataContextName)) {
                            $result.Add($dataContextName, ('{0}/$entity' -f $results.'@odata.context'))
                        }
                    } else {
                        if (![bool]$results.PSObject.Properties[$dataContextName]) {
                            $result | Add-Member -MemberType NoteProperty -Name $dataContextName -Value ('{0}/$entity' -f $results.'@odata.context')
                        }
                    }
                    Write-Output $result
                }
            } else { Write-Output $results }
        }

        function Complete-Result ($results, $DisablePaging) {
            if (!$DisablePaging -and $results -and (Get-ObjectProperty $results '@odata.nextLink')) {
                # The "skipToken" are in rare cases not unique, so when it is processed, we can end up in a caching loop. By updating the cache with the original uri with the final result, we workaround this issue and have a faster cache.
                $resultList = New-Object -TypeName System.Collections.ArrayList
                $resultList.AddRange(@($results.value))
                do {
                    $results = Invoke-MtGraphRequestCache -Method $($Method) -Uri $results.'@odata.nextLink' -Headers @{ ConsistencyLevel = $ConsistencyLevel } -OutputType $OutputType -DisableCache # Do not use cache as "skipTokens" is not always unique in large datasets and we may end with a loop
                    $resultList.AddRange(@($results.value))
                } while (Get-ObjectProperty $results '@odata.nextLink')
                $results.value = $resultList
                # Update the original request cache with the consolidated results
                if (!$DisableCache) {
                    $__MtSession.GraphCache[$uriQueryEndpointFinal.Uri.AbsoluteUri] = $results
                }
            }
            Format-Result $results $DisablePaging
        }
    }

    process {
        ## Initialize
        $results = $null

        if (!$UniqueId) { [string[]] $UniqueId = '' }
        if ($DisableBatching -and ($RelativeUri.Count -gt 1 -or $UniqueId.Count -gt 1)) {
            Write-Warning ('This command is invoking {0} individual Graph requests. For better performance, remove the -DisableBatching parameter.' -f ($RelativeUri.Count * $UniqueId.Count))
        }

        ## Process Each RelativeUri
        foreach ($uri in $RelativeUri) {
            $uriQueryEndpoint = New-Object System.UriBuilder -ArgumentList ([IO.Path]::Combine($GraphBaseUri.AbsoluteUri, $ApiVersion, $uri))

            ## Combine query parameters from URI and cmdlet parameters
            if ($uriQueryEndpoint.Query) {
                [hashtable] $finalQueryParameters = ConvertFrom-QueryString $uriQueryEndpoint.Query -AsHashtable
                if ($QueryParameters) {
                    foreach ($ParameterName in $QueryParameters.Keys) {
                        $finalQueryParameters[$ParameterName] = $QueryParameters[$ParameterName]
                    }
                }
            } elseif ($QueryParameters) { [hashtable] $finalQueryParameters = $QueryParameters }
            else { [hashtable] $finalQueryParameters = @{ } }
            if ($Select) { $finalQueryParameters['$select'] = $Select -join ',' }
            if ($Filter) { $finalQueryParameters['$filter'] = $Filter }
            $uriQueryEndpoint.Query = ConvertTo-QueryString $finalQueryParameters

            ## Invoke graph requests individually or save for single batch request
            foreach ($id in $UniqueId) {
                $uriQueryEndpointFinal = New-Object System.UriBuilder -ArgumentList $uriQueryEndpoint.Uri
                $uriQueryEndpointFinal.Path = ([IO.Path]::Combine($uriQueryEndpointFinal.Path, $id))

                if (!$DisableBatching -and ($RelativeUri.Count -gt 1 -or $UniqueId.Count -gt 1)) {
                    ## Create batch request entry
                    $request = New-Object PSObject -Property @{
                        id      = $listRequests.Count #(New-Guid).ToString()
                        method  = $($Method)
                        url     = $uriQueryEndpointFinal.Uri.AbsoluteUri -replace ('^{0}' -f [regex]::Escape($VersionedBaseUri)), ''
                        headers = @{ ConsistencyLevel = $ConsistencyLevel }
                    }
                    $listRequests.Add($request)
                } else {
                    # The cache key stays absolute, which is what keeps entries from one
                    # environment from being served to another.
                    $results = Invoke-MtGraphRequestCache -Method $($Method) -Uri (Resolve-TransportUri $uriQueryEndpointFinal.Uri) -CacheKey $uriQueryEndpointFinal.Uri.AbsoluteUri -Headers @{ ConsistencyLevel = $ConsistencyLevel } -OutputType $OutputType -DisableCache:$DisableCache -Body $Body
                    Complete-Result $results $DisablePaging
                }
            }
        }
    }

    end {
        if ($listRequests.Count -gt 0) {
            $uriQueryEndpoint = New-Object System.UriBuilder -ArgumentList ([IO.Path]::Combine($GraphBaseUri.AbsoluteUri, $ApiVersion, '$batch'))
            for ($iRequest = 0; $iRequest -lt $listRequests.Count; $iRequest += $BatchSize) {
                $indexEnd = [System.Math]::Min($iRequest + $BatchSize - 1, $listRequests.Count - 1)
                $jsonRequests = New-Object psobject -Property @{ requests = $listRequests[$iRequest..$indexEnd] } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
                Write-Debug $jsonRequests

content.text:
I've opened [#2629](https://github.com/maester365/maester/pull/2629) off main. A batched Graph request that fails no longer drops objects silently. The full unit test suite passes, apart from the usual ZeroTrustAssessment failure, but I haven't tried the fix against a real tenant yet. CI is still running.

**What `Invoke-MtGraphRequest` now does with each request in a batch:**
- **Throttled (429, 503, 504):** it sends that request again after the wait Graph asks for, up to three retries. Without a wait from Graph it backs off for 2, 4 and then 8 seconds, and it caps a wait at 60 seconds. Only the throttled requests are sent again.
- **Not found (404):** it returns nothing. Until now, the caller got an error object in place of the missing user or group.
- **Any other failure, or still throttled after the last retry:** it stops with an error that names the request, the status and the Graph error code. The check then shows an error instead of reporting on part of the data.

It also fixes a smaller ordering bug. Responses were sorted by their ids as text, so request 10 came before request 2. They now come back in request order.

**Tests:** six new tests cover the 404 skip, the 403 and 400 errors, a retry that waits as Graph asks, the back-off when Graph gives no wait, and giving up after four attempts. All six fail on main.

**What might change in runs:** a check that batches users or groups and lacks a permission will now show an error instead of passing on part of the data. That applies to seven checks, including ASD.ISM-1648, CIS 1.1.1 and CIS 1.2.2. That's the intent, but it could turn a pass into an error for a tenant that was hitting this without knowing it.

To check it for real, run the two Maester runs in parallel again on this branch. ASD.ISM-1648 should list all nine users, or show an error if Graph is still throttling after the retries.

input.recap: The #2629 run matches main on all 909 results, and ASD.ISM-1648 lists all nine users in both. The run was three minutes slower: two batched checks waited about 60 and 125 seconds, which fits throttled retries that then succeeded. I couldn't see the verbose retry lines to confirm.

content.text:
#2629 looks right: it got throttled and still reported correctly. Both runs match on all 909 results, and ASD.ISM-1648 lists all nine users in both. The remaining text differences are the same harmless ones as before: the MT.1092 `id`, and the MT.1178 row order.

**The timing shows the retries working.** The #2629 run took 7:37, against 4:40 for main, and two checks account for nearly all of that:

| Check | Main | #2629 |
|---|---|---|
| CIS.M365.1.1.1 | 4.5 s | 129.1 s |
| ASD.ISM-1648 | 0.2 s | 60.4 s |

Both read users in a batch. 60 seconds is the cap on a single wait, so ASD.ISM-1648 waited once and CIS 1.1.1 waited twice. Without the fix, those throttled users would have dropped out of both reports. With it, each check waited, retried, and produced exactly the same result as main. The #2629 run started a few minutes after main, so it hit the tenant while it was busiest, and main got through unthrottled this time.

I couldn't see your console, so I haven't seen the "Graph throttled … Retrying" lines myself. If they're still on screen, they'll show the waits. Either way, the durations match the code's waits too closely to be a coincidence.

One trade-off to decide on: a throttled check can now take up to three minutes, from three waits capped at 60 seconds each. That's slow, but the alternative was a quietly wrong report. If you'd rather keep runs short, I could lower the cap. A check would then error sooner when Graph is busy, rather than wait for it.
